query: Earlier automotive-catalyst research reported that Cu–Ni catalysts can oxidize CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures without platinum-group metals, while Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu catalysts can resist poisoning by H2O and NO and enable oxidation below 150 °C. Multi-principal-element catalysts in nearly equiatomic ratios have also been explored as a framework for combining high activity, thermal stability, and reduced platinum-group-metal use. These prior results demonstrate individual capabilities but do not establish the combined performance demanded by increasingly stringent regulations: clean exhaust during transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime despite the mileage-related degradation observed in real-driving-emission studies. Starting from a near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst, what single intervention could address this combined activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability problem without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention, explaining how it would work, predicting the change relative to the unmodified catalyst, defining the exhaust and aging conditions over which it should apply, citing supporting prior evidence, and specifying an experiment whose result would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Overlaying a thin, porous high‐entropy oxide (HEO) layer onto a near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element automotive alloy catalyst will enhance its low‐temperature oxidation activity, resistance to poisoning by H2O and NO, and long‐term durability without increasing platinum‐group metal loading by promoting multicomponent mixing that stabilizes active site dispersion and facilitates the formation of oxygen vacancies.
generation.material_initial_state: A near‐equiatomic, multi‐principal‐element alloy catalyst containing minimal platinum-group metals that currently exhibits moderate activity and durability but suffers from nanoparticle sintering and poisoning under transient, low‐temperature, and humid exhaust conditions.
generation.intervention: Deposit an ultrathin, porous HEO overlayer (engineered via techniques such as electrospinning or controlled sol–gel processing) onto the alloy catalyst to increase configurational disorder at the surface/support interface.
generation.conditions: Catalytic testing under simulated automotive exhaust conditions including transient low temperatures (below 150 °C as referenced in the question), exposure to moderate amounts of H2O vapor and NO, and thermal aging at high temperatures as defined by automotive standards.
generation.structural_mediator: The porous HEO layer, with its high configurational entropy and tailored nanopore architecture, acts as a sinter‐resistant scaffold that anchors active metal nanoparticles, maintaining a stable, high‐dispersion active site distribution.
generation.mechanism: By increasing the configurational disorder through multicomponent mixing, the HEO layer lowers the system's overall Gibbs free energy, suppressing nanoparticle sintering and growth, reducing the driving force for structural collapse under high temperatures and moisture, and creating oxygen vacancies that mitigate poisoning by facilitating reactant adsorption and oxygen mobility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified catalyst, the HEO‐modified catalyst is predicted to achieve full CO conversion at noticeably lower temperatures (e.g., a ~10–20% reduction in light‐off temperatures), retain high activity over extended operation (>300 hours) under moist conditions, and display reduced nanoparticle agglomeration.
generation.baseline: The unmodified near‐equiatomic alloy catalyst shows higher oxidation onset temperatures (e.g., T10 significantly above 150 °C), marked deactivation upon thermal aging, and significant nanoparticle sintering under similar conditions.
generation.boundary: The anticipated improvements apply to operation under typical automotive exhaust conditions with transient low-temperature periods, modest water vapor (up to 10 vol%), and aging up to approximately 900 °C. Performance improvements under more extreme conditions remain uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: While prior studies on high-entropy oxide supports and increased configurational disorder suggest enhanced stability and activity, the exact quantitative improvement in light-off temperatures, long-term durability, and sintering suppression must be validated. Potential interfacial interactions between the HEO overlayer and the alloy core under dynamic exhaust conditions also warrant further exploration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two catalyst samples: one consisting of the unmodified near-equiatomic alloy catalyst and the other with an ultrathin, porous HEO overlayer deposited onto the alloy. Subject both samples to CO oxidation tests under simulated automotive exhaust conditions that include transient operation at temperatures below 150 °C, exposure to 10 vol% water vapor and NO, and accelerated thermal aging (e.g., repeated heating cycles up to 900 °C). Before and after aging, analyze nanoparticle size distribution via HAADF-STEM and measure catalytic conversion temperatures (e.g., T10 and T50) as well as long-term activity over 300 hours.
measurements: Light-off temperatures (T10, T50) for CO oxidation
Activity retention (% conversion over time under simulated exhaust conditions)
Nanoparticle size distribution and dispersion via electron microscopy
Resistance to poisoning evaluated by performance under added H2O and NO
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEO-modified catalyst fails to demonstrate a statistically significant improvement (e.g., less than ~10% reduction in light-off temperatures, no measurable enhancement in long-term activity, or no reduction in nanoparticle sintering) compared to the unmodified catalyst under identical test conditions, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractEnhancing the activity and stability of earth‐abundant, heterogeneous catalysts remains a key challenge, requiring new materials design strategies to replace platinum‐group metals. Herein, it is demonstrated that increasing the configurational disorder of spinel metal oxides (M3O4, where M is a combination of Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, and Zn) leads to significant improvements in carbon monoxide (CO) oxidation performance. A substantial 63% decrease in the T10 value (temperature to reach 10% CO oxidation) is observed by systematically increasing the number of first‐row transition metals within the spinel oxide. Long‐term stability studies reveal that the most disordered 7‐metal spinel oxide exhibited superior resistance to catalyst deactivation compared to the 4‐metal variant, showing a decrease in activity of only 4.7% versus 12.2% during 14 h of operation. A solventless thermolysis approach is developed to synthesize a series of medium entropy spinel oxide (MESO) and high entropy spinel oxides (HESOs) from discrete, air‐stable molecular precursors. cited_evidence.text: These results underline the exceptional thermal stability of Pt nanoparticles, which is attributed to the high‐entropy effect. As shown in Figure 4g, the Pt/HEO‐850 °C catalyst demonstrated excellent stability during CO oxidation at 210 °C, maintaining consistent activity over 338 h with ignorable decline (Table S3, Supporting Information). The Pt/HEO‐850 °C demonstrates a slight decline (2.4%) in the 30‐h running with a low deactivation rate constant (k d) of 3.2 × 10−3 h−1, compared with recent Pt‐based catalysts (Figure 4h).[  ] This result exceeds the thermal stability conventional catalysts, showcasing its superior sinter‐resistance. To simulate hydrothermal conditions, vapor was introduced during testing, and even after 35 consecutive cycles, ignorable performance declines were observed (Figure 4i). In the 36th cycle, the porous structure remained intact, with the Pt nanoparticle size increasing only by 0.1–2.7 nm (Figures S36 and S37, Supporting Information). The durability of Pt/HEO in moisture‐rich environments, such as automotive exhaust systems, underscores its potential as a highly reliable catalyst for CO oxidation.
